content: This document is an updated Cochrane Review that evaluates the use of antihistamines, decongestants, or their combination in treating otitis media with effusion (OME) in children. OME is a common condition that can lead to hearing loss and developmental delays. However, the treatment of OME remains a subject of debate. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted to assess whether these medications are effective in resolving the effusion. The objective of this review was to determine the efficacy of antihistamines, decongestants, or their combination in managing OME in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, and others. The most recent search was completed on February 1, 2011, following an earlier search in 2006. The review included RCTs that specifically investigated the use of these medications for OME in children. Studies focusing on acute otitis media (AOM) were excluded, even if OME was assessed during follow-up. Data extraction and quality assessment of the included studies were performed independently by two authors using standardized methods. Dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals, applying a fixed-effect model for homogeneous data and a random-effects model for heterogeneous data. Continuous outcomes were discussed qualitatively. Statistical analyses were conducted using RevMan 5.1 software. The review included 16 studies with a total of 1,880 participants. The findings revealed no statistical or clinical benefit from the use of antihistamines, decongestants, or their combination in treating OME. Furthermore, children who received these treatments experienced 11% more side effects compared to those who did not receive treatment. The number needed to treat to harm (NNTH) was calculated to be 9, indicating that for every nine children treated, one would experience harm due to side effects. Based on the pooled data, the authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of antihistamines, decongestants, or their combination in managing OME in children. Additionally, the potential for harm outweighs any perceived benefit. Therefore, the authors recommend against the use of these medications for this condition.
